questions.question: Which statement best describes cloud computing?

options.text: Delivering computing services over the internet, on demand, typically paying for what you use
options.why: Correct. This is the core definition: services over the internet, on demand, metered.

options.text: Buying servers and installing them in your own building
options.why: That is the on-premises model, the opposite of cloud computing.

options.text: Storing files only on a USB drive so they are portable
options.why: Local storage is not delivered as a service over a network.

options.text: A single powerful supercomputer owned by Microsoft
options.why: The cloud is huge pools of servers across many datacenters, not one machine.

questions.explanation: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, networking and other services over the internet, usually with consumption-based pricing.

questions.question: Which TWO are characteristics of cloud computing?

options.why: Correct. You provision resources yourself, in minutes, without a purchase process.

options.text: Long-term hardware purchase contracts are required
options.why: Cloud removes the need to buy hardware. Commitments such as reservations are optional.
Correct. Usage is metered and billed based on consumption.

options.text: Capacity can only be changed by buying new servers
options.why: Rapid elasticity means capacity changes quickly without buying hardware.

questions.explanation: On-demand self-service and measured service are two of the five essential characteristics (with broad network access, resource pooling and rapid elasticity).

questions.scenario: A ticket-booking start-up expects huge traffic for one concert sale and almost none afterwards. It does not want to buy servers.
questions.question: Why is cloud computing a good fit?

options.text: It can add capacity for the sale and release it afterwards, so they pay mainly for what they use
options.why: Correct. Rapid elasticity plus consumption-based pricing suit short, spiky demand.

options.text: Cloud servers are free during traffic spikes
options.why: Cloud resources are not free. You pay for the capacity you consume.

options.text: The cloud removes the need for any application code
options.why: You still build the application. The cloud provides the infrastructure and services.
No provider guarantees zero downtime. Availability is defined by SLAs.

questions.explanation: Spiky, temporary demand is the textbook case for cloud: scale out for the event, scale in afterwards, pay for actual usage.

questions.question: In a public cloud such as Azure, who is responsible for the physical datacenter and its hardware?

options.why: Customers never manage physical datacenters in the public cloud.
Correct. Microsoft owns, operates and secures Azure's physical datacenters.
The ISP provides connectivity, not the cloud datacenter.
Physical security is always the provider's job in public cloud (see the shared responsibility model).

questions.explanation: Physical hosts, network and datacenter are always the cloud provider's responsibility in the public cloud.
